body.alt: Colorado Wrongful Death Statute of Limitations

children.text: Colorado law allows certain family members to bring a civil lawsuit when another party’s negligence or wrongful conduct causes a fatal injury. These claims arise from many different circumstances, yet all follow the same core legal framework that controls who may file, what compensation may be available, and how long the family has to act.
What Is a Wrongful Death Claim?
A
wrongful death claim

allows eligible family members to seek civil compensation when a person’s death results from another party’s negligence, recklessness, or intentional misconduct. Instead of focusing on the harm suffered by the deceased, Colorado wrongful death law centers on the losses experienced by surviving family members, including financial hardship and the loss of companionship, guidance, and emotional support. Families researching the
wrongful death statute of limitations in Colorado
often start with this distinction because filing rights and deadlines depend on who the law recognizes as a proper claimant.
These civil cases move forward independently of any criminal prosecution. Even when the state brings charges,
a wrongful death lawsuit

follows a separate process and seeks compensation rather than punishment. Families commonly pursue these claims after fatal traffic crashes, medical errors, unsafe property conditions, defective products, workplace incidents, or institutional neglect, all situations where a duty of care existed and failed.
What Is the Colorado Wrongful Death Statute?

Colorado’s wrongful death law, commonly known as the Colorado Wrongful Death Act, establishes the right to bring a civil lawsuit when a death results from another party’s wrongful conduct. According to
Colorado Revised Statutes section 13-21-201

, liability may arise when a fatal injury occurs due to negligence, unskillfulness, or criminal intent tied to transportation operations or employment-related conduct, allowing surviving family members to pursue compensation through the civil court system.

This statute forms the legal foundation for wrongful death claims across Colorado and defines when responsibility attaches to employers, corporations, or individuals whose actions or omissions cause a fatal injury. While the statutory language is detailed, its purpose remains straightforward, providing a legal path for families to seek accountability after a preventable death.
Common Situations That Result in Wrongful Death Lawsuits
Wrongful death lawsuits in Colorado often arise from everyday circumstances where preventable harm occurs. Common situations include:
Motor vehicle accidents:
Fatal crashes involving cars, trucks, motorcycles, bicycles, or pedestrians, frequently tied to speeding, impaired driving, or distraction.
Medical malpractice:
Deadly diagnostic errors, delayed treatment, surgical mistakes, or failures in post-procedure monitoring.
Premises liability:
Unsafe property conditions such as poor lighting, missing railings, hazardous walkways, or unaddressed fall risks that lead to fatal injuries.
Defective products:
Design flaws, manufacturing defects, or missing warnings that cause a product to become unreasonably dangerous.
Workplace accidents:
Unsafe equipment, hazardous exposure, or inadequate safety practices that result in fatal on-the-job injuries.
Institutional abuse or neglect:
Preventable deaths in nursing homes or long-term care facilities caused by neglect, dehydration, infections, or poor supervision.
Criminal acts:
Assault, homicide, or other intentional conduct that may lead to both criminal prosecution and a separate civil wrongful death claim.
Because evidence in these cases can disappear quickly, understanding deadlines and early investigation often plays a decisive role.
How Long Do You Have to File a Wrongful Death Claim in Colorado?
Most Colorado wrongful death claims must be filed within two years of the date of death. This two-year window sits at the heart of the
wrongful death statute of limitations in Colorado
and generally controls whether a claim may proceed.

Certain circumstances can affect how the filing period applies. Some motor vehicle cases follow different statutory rules, and claims involving government entities may require early notice well before the two-year mark. Families should never assume extra time applies without confirmation, since courts strictly enforce these deadlines.
Who Can File a Denver Wrongful Death Claim?

Colorado law limits who may file a wrongful death lawsuit, and eligibility depends on both family relationship and timing after the death. These rules often surprise families, especially during the first year.

During the first year following death, the surviving spouse usually holds the exclusive right to file, with the ability to include children or designate another party. After the first year, surviving children gain independent filing rights. When no spouse or children exist, parents may file, and recent legislative changes expanded eligibility to include siblings in certain circumstances, which can matter when a sibling serves as the closest remaining family member.
Recovering Compensation from a Wrongful Death Lawsuit

Wrongful death compensation addresses the financial and personal impact families face after losing a loved one. While money never replaces a life, it can help protect a household from cascading financial harm. Families navigating the
wrongful death statute of limitations in Colorado
also need to
understand damages early
, since documentation gathered near the beginning of a case often shapes recovery later.

Compensation may include medical expenses tied to the fatal injury, funeral and burial costs, and the loss of future income or benefits. Non-economic damages may cover losses such as companionship, emotional support, and the relationship the family expected to continue.
Under
House Bill 24-1472

, approved June 3, 2024, and effective January 1, 2025, Colorado increased noneconomic damage limits in medical malpractice cases on a phased schedule toward $875,000, with future inflation adjustments, reflecting a broader recognition of these personal losses.
What Is the Difference Between a Wrongful Death Lawsuit and a Survival Action?

A wrongful death lawsuit compensates surviving family members for their losses, while a survival action seeks damages the deceased could have recovered had they lived. Colorado law recognizes both claims, and families may pursue them together in appropriate cases.

A survival action focuses on harms suffered by the deceased between injury and death, such as pain, suffering, and lost wages, with recovery passing through the estate. A wrongful death claim addresses the losses the family experiences after death, including financial support and emotional connection.
